A FIELD GUIDE TO YOUR LITTLE TROUBLEMAKER

Gluttony.

When one more stops being more fun.

You know how to enjoy a good thing. Your inner enthusiast brings delight and abundance, but occasionally misses the moment when “lovely” becomes “a bit much.”

THE SHORT VERSION

What does gluttony mean?

In our quiz, gluttony is the just-one-more loop: continuing to consume something after the enjoyable part has started to fade. Some questions use entertainment and scrolling as modern analogies. The focus is the gap between what you want to enjoy and what keeps happening on autopilot, not how much pleasure you are allowed to have.

The good energy

You make room for pleasure and help everyday moments feel like occasions.

The little tripwire

A comforting habit can keep going after it stops feeling good.

SUSPICIOUSLY FAMILIAR?

Little moments.
Recognizable habits.

These are illustrations, not extra test questions. One familiar moment does not define you.

The autoplay decision

You are no longer following the story, but the next episode starts before you decide whether you actually want to watch it.

The disappearing break

You open an app for a little entertainment. Later, you realize most of the break was spent looking for something more interesting than the last thing.

The automatic extra

You reach for another helping of a favorite activity because it is there, then notice it is not adding much to the experience anymore.

ROOM FOR NUANCE

Enjoyment and the automatic extra

Enjoying food, rest, games, or a long evening with friends is not a failing. This character asks whether continuing is still a choice you enjoy. It is not a measure of body size, diet, eating behavior, addiction, or health.

IF THIS CHARACTER SHOWED UP IN YOUR RESULT

Read the score.
Keep the context.

A higher gluttony score

A higher gluttony score means our statements about continuing past enjoyment fit more closely. You might reflect on what makes it easy to pause or difficult to stop in a particular setting. The score does not identify a health condition.

A lower gluttony score

A lower score means the few just-one-more situations we selected felt less familiar. It does not prove superior self-control, and it says nothing about what or how much you should eat.

How the number works

Each tendency has three equally weighted questions, answered from 0 to 4. Balancing statements are reverse-scored. The total out of 12 is converted to a rounded score out of 100. Your seven scores are independent; they do not add up to 100. A tie stays a tie.

A score is not a population percentile, a diagnosis, or a fixed personality type. Read the scoring explanation.

A SMALL EXPERIMENT

A little more temperance.

Choose a low-stakes activity such as watching clips or browsing a shop. At a natural stopping point, pause and ask whether you want more of that exact experience. Continuing deliberately and choosing something else are both possible answers.

Three questions to sit with

  • Am I still enjoying this, or waiting for it to become enjoyable again?
  • What did I hope this break would give me?
  • If I paused now, what would I choose to do next?

No perfect answer required. Pick the question that feels useful and leave the rest.

BEFORE YOU MAKE IT YOUR WHOLE PERSONALITY

Good questions.

Does gluttony mean eating a lot?

The traditional word is associated with excess in eating and drinking. Our entertainment quiz also uses everyday consumption as an analogy. It should not be used to judge appetite, weight, or food choices.

Can this score tell me if I have an eating disorder or an addiction?

No. These three questions cannot assess either. The page is a reflection on ordinary habits, not a screening tool or treatment guide.
